issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Institutional Failure: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening motor vehicle collision, 'institutional failure' and especially 'betrayal by someone trusted' are hard to reconcile unless the crash involved unusual interpersonal circumstances not reflected anywhere else in the profile. The rest of the profile centers on fear/startle/intrusive sensory recall, which fits an accident trauma; these appraisal items instead imply an interpersonal or systemic-trauma narrative.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted
issues.explanation: 'Guilt on recall' can occur after accidents, but in this profile it sits awkwardly with the chosen appraisal set: the appraisals focus on betrayal/institutional failure rather than self-blame or responsibility. That makes the guilt theme insufficiently supported across nodes for a coherent cognitive formulation.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening motor vehicle collision, the appraisal 'I was betrayed by someone I trusted' is hard to reconcile unless the crash specifically involved a trusted driver or intentional wrongdoing, which is not otherwise reflected anywhere else in the profile. As presented, it introduces a different interpersonal-trauma theme that is not supported by the rest of the selected items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: Within Negative Appraisals, 'Betrayal' and 'Self-Blame' can sometimes coexist, but in this profile they point to different causal narratives for the trauma (trusted other's betrayal vs one's own actions causing the event) without any supporting context. That makes the appraisal set clinically hard to unify around a single MVC trauma narrative.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Other-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what other people have done to me
issues.explanation: The profile contains a hard-to-reconcile blame pattern: strong self-blame and guilt are paired with other-blame rumination as a core maladaptive strategy. Mixed blame can occur, but this combination is the main internal inconsistency in the selected items because the appraisals and memory items point toward inward blame, while the strategy item points toward sustained outward blame.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: Within the cognitive formulation, Maladaptive Strategies links most strongly to Negative Appraisals, so the strategy content should fit the appraisal style. Here the appraisal style is dominated by self-blame, helplessness, and permanent emotional damage, making other-blame rumination the least coherent strategy item.

issues.item: Memory: Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening motor vehicle collision, guilt on recall is plausible, especially with self-blame, so it is not problematic by itself. The concern is specifically its combination with persistent other-blame rumination, which pulls the profile toward a different blame direction than the rest of the formulation.

vignette: Juan Hernandez's eyes still flash with a dancer's intensity, but his movements have lost their fluidity. At 62, he has spent decades mastering the rhythms of salsa and tango, performing for crowds across Latin America and the United States. But since the night his car skidded off a rain-soaked highway, sending him careening into a concrete median, Juan's life has been marked by a different kind of movement – the frantic effort to escape his memories. That night still replays in vivid sensory fragments: the screech of tires, the crunch of metal, and the eerie silence that followed. Juan tries not to think about it, but the sounds and images seep into his mind like a slow-moving fog. When they do, he deliberately blanks out, leaving his body as if hovering above the scene. It's a trick he's learned to cope with the horror of what happened – a way to temporarily flee from the memories that haunt him. As a dancer, Juan's sense of rhythm and timing once guided him through life. Now, it feels like an enemy. He finds himself scanning rooms for exits as soon as he enters them, his eyes darting towards doors and windows with a nervous intensity. His wife, Ana, has noticed the change in him – how he startles at her touch, even when she's just trying to hold his hand. Juan knows it's irrational, but the sudden contact makes him feel like he's back on that rain-soaked highway, fighting for control. Sleep has become a luxury Juan can ill afford. He stays up late into the night, sometimes watching TV or scrolling through his phone until exhaustion finally claims him. It's not just the memories that keep him awake – it's the shame that accompanies them. When he recalls the accident, he feels an overwhelming sense of responsibility, as if he was somehow to blame for the whole thing. Juan's dance troupe has noticed his withdrawal, too. He used to be their lead choreographer, but now he finds himself struggling to come up with new routines. It's not just a lack of inspiration – it's the fear that he'll never be able to feel normal emotions again. The music that once moved him so deeply now feels hollow, like a distant echo from another life. Ana has tried to reassure Juan that he's still the same person, but deep down, he knows she doesn't understand. To him, the accident was more than just a random event – it was a manifestation of his own flaws. He's convinced that if only he had been more careful, more vigilant, the whole thing could have been avoided. As Juan navigates this new reality, he feels like he's lost control over his life. The world seems full of threats, from the crowded streets to the intimate spaces of his home. Ana tries to reach out to him, but Juan pushes her away, unsure of how to explain what's happening inside his head. It was Ana who finally convinced Juan to seek help, after months of watching him struggle in silence. As he sits in the therapist's office, Juan feels a glimmer of hope – maybe, just maybe, he can learn to confront these memories and emotions without running away from them. But what if it's too late? What if he's lost forever in this sea of shame and fear? The thought sends a shiver down his spine, a reminder that the journey ahead will be long and difficult, but perhaps – just perhaps – not impossible.
